title: Regulated

brief.story: The sensor board runs on 5 V, but the bench gives 9 V. An LM7805 regulator turns any 7–25 V into a steady 5 V. Its ground wire and the LED circuit on its output are in; the regulator isn’t.
brief.goal: Fit the LM7805 so its output (column 7) is 4.9–5.1 V and LED1 carries 10–16 mA.

hints: Take the regulator from the bar and click column 5: its legs land in 5 (IN), 6 (GND) and 7 (OUT).
IN gets the 9 V feed (column 5), GND is wired to ground (column 6), and OUT feeds R1 (column 7).
On 5 V the LED gets (5 − 2) ÷ 220 = 13.6 mA. Wired straight to 9 V instead it would take 32 mA and burn.

spec.explain: R1 was sized for 5 V: (5 − 2) ÷ 220 = 13.6 mA. On 9 V the same resistor lets 32 mA through.

debrief: A linear regulator holds its output at a fixed voltage whatever the input does, by burning the difference as heat: here (9 − 5) V × 14 mA = 56 mW. Every Arduino and USB gadget has one between its supply and its chips, which is why a 9 V battery can safely run 5 V logic.
